title: Brisk and the Sunpetal Quest
markdown:
The sun, warm and gold, peeked over the jagged peaks of Sunspike and laid dancing shadows across whispering pines. Brisk the young goblin practised pebble-skipping on a tumbling stream that babbled like a happy secret. His pointed ears twitched with delight. Beside him Echo, a sleek bat of velvet darkness with ears that caught the slightest sound, swooped and twirled, squeaks like tiny musical notes. Pine needles. Damp earth. Safe, known, home.

Grandma Grizelda’s birthday was around the corner. Only Sunpetal flowers, blooming on the highest rocky ledges, would do. He pictured her smile lighting her whole face, wrinkled kind hands arranging golden petals in a favourite chipped vase. He must find them. A tiny tremor rippled through small green hands. He always felt a prickle when he went too far from the cozy burrow. Paws a little clammy. Tummy a little flip-flop. He went anyway.

The Sunpetals grew on windy paths that hugged the edge of Sunspike. The wind whistled, carrying mountain birds and wild thyme. Ordinary daisies from the garden would not do. He had promised the very best.

A twisty rocky path. The cheerful whistling of the wind changed to a rather uncheerful grumbling. Rounding a bend, Brisk’s eyes widened. In a small sun-drenched clearing carpeted with soft moss stood a wizard and a witch, locked in a most peculiar argument. Fizzwick the Wizard, long wispy beard tickling his chin, spectacles perched precariously, wrung his hands as if they were lost socks. Morwenna the Witch, pointy hat adorned with jingling bells bobbing indignantly, pointed a gnarled finger, her voice sharp and clear.

“You simply must have seen it. My very best shimmering-blue teacup. Dancing moonbeams painted on it. Gone.”

“I haven’t touched it. Perfectly pleasant morning with chamomile and moonbeam biscuits. Not a teacup in sight. Only my own, decidedly less blue, mug.”

Disagreements made Brisk’s tummy feel like tangled yarn. He wanted to scurry invisible among grey rocks. Echo clung to his shoulder and chirped, a comforting rumble: stay and see.

Morwenna sighed, bells jingling exasperation. “It was on this mossy stone, waiting for dandelion delight. Perhaps you saw it, little goblin? It shines rather brilliantly.”

Brisk shuffled. Worn boots on moss. “N-no, ma’am. But my Grandma Grizelda needs Sunpetal flowers. They grow up there.”

Fizzwick’s spectacles slid further. “Sunpetals. Magnificent. Sun-kissed spots. Rather difficult to reach.” He peered at his feet. “Wait. My biscuits were particularly crumbly this morning.”

Tucked behind Fizzwick’s voluminous star-spangled robe, peeking from midnight-blue fabric: a shimmering blue teacup, dried moonbeam dust around the rim. Fallen, perhaps, while he used it as a crumb catcher.

Brisk took a small step. Courage like a tiny warm ember. “Excuse me, Mr. Wizard? Is that your teacup?”

Fizzwick’s eyes widened. “Oh my stars and moonbeams!” He pulled it free. Morwenna’s. Absorbed in biscuits and tidying, he had set it down as one might a spare sock. “I am dreadfully sorry. My mind was contemplating biscuit structure.”

Morwenna’s relief jingle was merry. “A shared cup of tea will smooth most misunderstandings. Especially dandelion delight.”

They looked at Brisk, who had, quite accidentally, solved the problem with a few brave words. Fizzwick rummaged and pressed a lumpy stone like a sleepy grey beetle into Brisk’s hand. “A pebble of pleasant persistence. It hums when you’re about to give up.”

It was not a Sunpetal. It would not make Grandmother smile like golden flowers. He hesitated, then managed a small polite smile. He had to leave them for the ledges. Wind tasted of ice. Rough granite scraped his knees. Distant laughter faded. He clutched the humming pebble, warmth through worn fabric, and scrambled on. The brief delay meant a stronger gust nearly unbalanced him on the narrow ledge.

Then a sun-drenched shelf, and there they were: Sunpetals, vibrant gold, each a tiny piece of captured sunshine. He gathered a bunch, paws nimble. The journey home felt easier. The pebble hummed in his pocket.

In the cozy burrow Grandma Grizelda’s face lit up, a smile as bright as the flowers themselves. She hugged him tight, smelling of lavender and old books, and set the petals in the chipped vase as if they had always belonged there. Later that evening, by the fire, baking bread in the air, Brisk noticed a tricky knot in his shoelace, the sort that usually made him sigh and stop. The pebble warmed against his leg, a subtle gentle vibration. He took a breath that tasted of the climb. Slowly, patiently, small green fingers worked. The knot came undone. Echo hung from a beam and squeaked once, as if he had known about knots all along. The unknown had not vanished entirely. But a little goblin and his bat could find their way through surprising ledges, armed with persistence, a few brave words, and a vase already waiting on the table.
